books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, A. Political Parties and the Rise of the First Two-Party System

stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801, public domain (Avalon Project text). Abridged with ellipses.
stimulus.text:
“Every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. … Equal and exact justice to all men, of whatever state or persuasion, religious or political; peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; the support of the State governments in all their rights, as the most competent administrations for our domestic concerns, and the surest bulwarks against anti-republican tendencies; the preservation of the General Government in its whole constitutional vigor, as the sheet anchor of our peace at home and safety abroad.”
— Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Jefferson's First Inaugural Address (1801)
stem: In the passage, Jefferson's claim that “we are all Republicans, we are all Federalists” most directly shows that he wanted to

options.text: merge the two parties into a single national party
options.misconception: Jefferson led the Democratic-Republicans and never tried to merge the parties; he wanted Federalists to accept his presidency, not to give up their party.

options.text: warn Federalists that they would be removed from office
options.misconception: Nothing in the line threatens Federalists with removal; Jefferson is reaching out to them, not warning them.

options.text: calm partisan anger by saying both parties shared republican principles
admit that the two parties agreed on every policy
options.misconception: Jefferson says the parties share principles, not policies; they still fought bitterly over the bank, taxes, and foreign affairs.

rationales.A: Jefferson led the Democratic-Republicans and never tried to merge the parties. He wanted Federalists to accept his presidency, not to give up their party.
rationales.B: Nothing in the line threatens Federalists with removal. Jefferson is reaching out to the losers, not warning them.
rationales.C: Jefferson calls the parties “brethren of the same principle” right after a bitter election, telling Federalists they are not enemies of the republic. The line is a peace offering, not a policy statement. Background: Federalists had warned that Jefferson would bring French-style terror, so he needed the losers to trust the transfer of power.
rationales.D: Jefferson says the parties share principles, not policies. The two sides still disagreed sharply over the bank, taxes, and foreign affairs.
rationales.general:
1. Read the line in its moment. Jefferson has just won a bitter election, and Federalists fear him.
2. Notice the word he chooses. “Brethren” means brothers, and “same principle” means both sides stand on republican ground.
3. Ask what the line does. It tells the losers they still belong in the republic, so they can accept defeat.
4. Put it together. A new president who won a nasty race uses his first speech to lower the temperature.
Remember: after a bitter election, a leader's first words often aim to calm the losers.
